rationale: AR amplification and overexpression are hallmark mechanisms of castration resistance. In Grasso et al. and similar cohorts, AR mRNA is markedly elevated in metastatic CRPC relative to localized, hormone-naive tumors, driven by AR gene amplification and adaptive upregulation under androgen deprivation. A minority of AR-negative, neuroendocrine-like CRPC samples exists, but overall AR mRNA should be significantly higher in CRPC.

EZH2 is a well-established marker of metastatic prostate cancer (Varambally 2002), and it is consistently overexpressed in metastatic CRPC compared with localized disease. It is also linked to proliferation and E2F activity, both of which are elevated in CRPC. Grasso et al. and similar datasets show higher EZH2 mRNA in mCRPC rapid-autopsy samples, so the same pattern is expected here.

AURKA is a proliferation/mitotic gene and is overexpressed in metastatic CRPC, especially in neuroendocrine variants (Beltran et al.). Mitotic genes are consistently upregulated in CRPC versus localized tumors in the Grasso and other cohorts, so AURKA should be higher in CRPC.

KLK3 is highly expressed in localized prostate tissue. Metastatic CRPC at autopsy is heterogeneous: some tumors have weakened canonical AR output after androgen deprivation, some are AR-low or neuroendocrine, and samples are diluted by non-prostatic host tissue (liver, node, bone). Many array datasets (Varambally, Chandran, Taylor) show reduced KLK3 in metastases despite AR amplification. This is recalled from related datasets, not verified in Grasso, so lower in CRPC is likely but uncertain.

expert_note: Dataset, not model: PSMA/FOLH1 is generally higher in mCRPC; the lower value here is specific to this array dataset. Reasonable prior.
rationale: FOLH1 encodes PSMA. Its expression is repressed by androgen signaling and rises with castration and progression. PSMA immunostaining and mRNA are consistently higher in metastatic CRPC than in primary tumors. Neuroendocrine or AR-null CRPC subsets may lose FOLH1, adding heterogeneity, but the overall trend in the Grasso CRPC samples should still be up.

SSTR1 is expressed in benign and localized prostate epithelium and stroma. Metastatic CRPC samples lack prostatic stroma and tend to lose differentiated-tissue transcripts. Reports describe reduced somatostatin receptor expression with progression, although neuroendocrine subsets could raise it. Overall, a modest decrease in metastatic CRPC seems most likely in this dataset, so confidence is only moderate.

rationale: SSTR2 is expressed in benign prostate epithelium, stroma and vasculature, and is reported to decrease with malignant progression. Most Grasso CRPC metastases are AR-driven adenocarcinomas rather than neuroendocrine tumors, where SSTR2 can rise. Loss of benign and stromal content in metastases, plus general downregulation of differentiation and tissue-context genes in CRPC, likely yields lower SSTR2 than in localized tumors. Confidence is modest because neuroendocrine cases could raise SSTR2.

expert_note: Model error: predicted a change where none was detected; over-predicts effects.
rationale: SST is expressed by scattered neuroendocrine cells and stromal/neural elements in primary prostate tissue, and it tends to fall in adenocarcinoma. Most Grasso CRPC metastases are AR-driven adenocarcinomas in non-prostatic sites that lack this microenvironment, so overall SST should be lower. This is uncertain: the few neuroendocrine CRPC cases could carry high SST and offset the trend.

TFF3 is strongly overexpressed in primary prostate cancer, especially ERG-negative tumors, and is partly hormone/AR-responsive. Many genes overexpressed in localized tumors, along with luminal differentiation markers, tend to decline in heterogeneous, heavily treated metastatic CRPC. Some CRPC tumors are also AR-low or neuroendocrine. So TFF3 is likely lower overall in CRPC in GSE35988, though its retention in some metastases makes this uncertain.

expert_note: Model error: ESR1 is strongly lower (FDR 2e-21); the model itself noted stromal ESR1 but weighted IHC reports of ERa in treated tumors.
rationale: AR signaling represses ESR1, so androgen deprivation is expected to derepress it. Immunohistochemistry studies (e.g., Bonkhoff) report ERα in high-grade, metastatic and hormone-treated prostate cancer. Some CRPC metastases also sit in ESR1-expressing host tissues such as liver. Against this, ESR1 in localized tumors is largely stromal, and dilution of that stroma in metastases could reduce the signal. The direction is therefore uncertain.

SRD5A2 is strongly expressed in prostate stroma and in benign or localized tissue, and it is AR-regulated. In metastatic CRPC, where stroma is largely absent, studies (Montgomery 2008, Stanbrough 2006) report SRD5A2 decreasing while SRD5A1 increases. In Grasso and similar datasets, SRD5A2 is markedly lower in metastases than in primary tumors.

NR3C1 is highly expressed in prostate stroma and benign epithelium. Prostatectomy samples carry substantial stromal content, whereas metastatic CRPC samples are more tumor-pure. Several metastasis datasets (Varambally, Chandran) report lower NR3C1 in metastases. Glucocorticoid co-treatment, common in CRPC, may also downregulate GR mRNA. Against this, ADT-induced GR upregulation in some CRPCs could raise levels, so the call is uncertain.

In adult prostate, PAGE4 is expressed mainly in stromal fibroblast and smooth-muscle cells; single-cell studies list it among prostate stromal markers. Localized prostatectomy samples contain abundant prostatic fibromuscular stroma. CRPC metastases in lymph node, liver or bone lack that stroma. The very large drop (about 115-fold) fits loss of prostate-specific stroma better than a change within tumor cells. Some epithelial PAGE4 loss with progression may contribute.

FCER1A encodes the high-affinity IgE receptor alpha chain, expressed by mast cells and basophils, not prostate epithelial cells. Prostatectomy samples include prostatic stroma rich in mast cells. Metastatic CRPC from autopsy sits in bone, liver, or lymph node with a different microenvironment and little prostatic stroma. The large drop therefore most likely reflects a loss of mast-cell and stromal content, not a change within the cancer cells.

In the prostate, SRD5A2 is expressed mainly in stromal cells and benign epithelium, and its level is already low in cancer epithelium. Localized prostatectomy samples include prostatic stroma. CRPC metastases (liver, lymph node, bone and others) lack that prostate-specific stroma. A 32-fold drop fits loss of SRD5A2-expressing non-tumor tissue, though a known tumor-intrinsic SRD5A2-to-SRD5A1 switch in CRPC may contribute.

PCP4 appears to be highly expressed in prostatic stromal and smooth-muscle (and neural) compartments. Primary prostatectomy tissue contains abundant fibromuscular stroma. Rapid-autopsy metastases (liver, lymph node, bone) lack prostate stroma. A drop this large (~28-fold) resembles the losses of stromal markers such as MYH11 and DES, which points to tissue composition. Some tumor-intrinsic change, such as AR-related reprogramming, cannot be excluded, and PCP4's prostate-specific expression pattern is uncertain.

ASB5 is a muscle-enriched gene (skeletal, smooth, and vascular muscle). Localized prostatectomy samples contain abundant fibromuscular stroma rich in smooth muscle. Metastatic CRPC lesions at sites such as liver, lymph node, and bone lack prostatic smooth muscle stroma. The very large drop (about 6 log2 units) fits loss of stromal or muscle content better than a change inside the cancer cells.

ACTBL2 (kappa-actin) is an actin-family gene, and large CRPC-versus-localized drops in this design are most often stromal or smooth-muscle genes. Prostatectomy samples include abundant fibromuscular prostate stroma, which metastatic deposits at various sites lack. Surgical ischemia and handling differences could also contribute. I am not certain ACTBL2 is stroma-enriched in prostate, so a tumor-intrinsic loss cannot be excluded.

expert_note: Label disputed: CD38 is expressed in benign luminal epithelium, which my composition scores do not model. Model reasoning is defensible.
rationale: CD38 is highly expressed in benign prostate luminal epithelium and in plasma cells and lymphocytes. Prostatectomy samples carry admixed benign glands and inflammatory infiltrate; distant CRPC metastases lack native prostate tissue. A drop of about 50-fold (-5.66 log2) fits loss of these non-cancer compartments better than regulation within cancer cells. Tumor-intrinsic CD38 loss has been reported, though, so this is uncertain.

A tumor-intrinsic alternative is plausible: UNC5D sits on 8p12, a region often deleted in prostate cancer, and is a putative tumor suppressor. But the size of the change favors composition. Uncertain.

DPP4 (CD26) is an androgen-regulated luminal epithelial gene that is highly expressed in localized prostate cancer cells. Published work (e.g., Enz et al.) shows AR-dependent DPP4 suppression in CRPC and enzalutamide resistance. Fibroblast and benign-gland DPP4 could add some composition effect in metastases, but the large drop fits loss or rewiring of canonical AR output in castration-resistant tumor cells under androgen deprivation.

A large, highly significant drop in metastatic CRPC fits loss of prostate-specific benign epithelium or stromal content: autopsy metastases lack the surrounding normal prostate tissue present in prostatectomy specimens, and they also differ in site and tissue handling. A tumor-intrinsic decrease, for example through loss of AR or luminal differentiation, cannot be excluded.

rationale: ATP8B4 is not a known AR target or CRPC driver. Its expression appears to come largely from non-epithelial cells, plausibly prostate stromal or smooth-muscle compartments, which make up much of radical prostatectomy samples. Metastatic CRPC deposits at distant sites lack prostatic stroma, so a large 14-fold drop fits a difference in tissue composition better than reprogramming within the cancer cells. This rests on uncertain recall of where ATP8B4 is expressed.

SLC22A4 (OCTN1) is expressed in prostate luminal epithelium rather than stroma or immune cells. Its loss in CRPC more plausibly reflects dedifferentiation or reprogramming of the cancer cells, like other prostate-differentiation genes, than stromal dilution. Some contribution from benign glands contaminating the prostatectomy samples is possible, which keeps confidence modest.

ARSI exposure selects for AR amplification, enhancer gain, and AR-V7 splice variants, all of which raise total AR transcript levels in most resistant mCRPC. A minority of AR-low or neuroendocrine tumors also emerge after ARSI, which could dilute the effect. On balance, the cohort-level comparison most likely shows higher AR mRNA in ARSI-exposed biopsies. This is a recall-based estimate, not checked against the dataset.

SSTR1 is expressed in prostate cancer but is not an established AR target. Its known neuroendocrine link is weaker than SSTR2's. ARSI exposure in this cohort is linked to lower AR signaling and modestly more NE features. Those changes might raise SSTR1 slightly, but after adjusting for biopsy site I would expect no robust difference. This is a guess from general knowledge, not recall of the paper's results.

rationale: EZH2 is an E2F/proliferation-linked gene that drives lineage plasticity and neuroendocrine transdifferentiation. Prior abiraterone or enzalutamide exposure enriches for AR-indifferent, NE-like and highly proliferative mCRPC phenotypes, and Abida et al. reported higher NE scores with ARSI exposure. A modest increase in EZH2 is therefore likely, though the effect may be small and might not reach significance after site adjustment.

DPP4 is a well-documented androgen/AR-regulated gene in prostate epithelium. Prior or ongoing abiraterone/enzalutamide exposure selects for tumors with attenuated canonical AR output, lineage plasticity, and neuroendocrine/AR-low phenotypes, which typically show reduced expression of AR-driven genes such as KLK3, NKX3-1, TMPRSS2 and DPP4. Hence I expect modestly lower DPP4 in ARSI-exposed mCRPC after adjusting for biopsy site, though effect size may be small.

ST6GALNAC1, which synthesizes the sialyl-Tn antigen, is a well-characterized androgen-induced gene in prostate cancer (Munkley et al.). Abida et al. reported reduced AR signaling scores and more AR-low or neuroendocrine phenotypes in ARSI-exposed mCRPC. AR-dependent targets like ST6GALNAC1 should therefore be modestly lower after abiraterone or enzalutamide. Heterogeneous AR reactivation means the effect may be small, possibly not significant.

TRPM8 is a classic androgen-regulated gene, directly induced by AR in prostate epithelium. Abiraterone and enzalutamide suppress canonical AR signaling, and ARSI exposure is associated with reduced AR-target scores and more AR-low or neuroendocrine phenotypes. TRPM8 is therefore expected to be lower in ARSI-exposed mCRPC biopsies, although AR reactivation in some tumors may weaken the difference.

CXCL11 is an interferon-induced chemokine that reflects immune infiltration, which varies widely between patients and biopsy sites. ARSI exposure mainly shifts AR-signaling and neuroendocrine/lineage programs. There is no strong known link between abiraterone or enzalutamide exposure and CXCL11 levels in mCRPC, so after adjusting for biopsy site the difference is most likely not significant. Some reports of interferon signaling after AR blockade make a modest increase possible.

rationale: GHR has been reported as androgen-responsive in prostate models. Sustained AR pathway inhibition from abiraterone or enzalutamide reduces AR-driven transcription in mCRPC, so modestly lower GHR in ARSI-exposed tumors is plausible. This is a weakly grounded guess: I am not confident GHR is a robust AR target, and the effect may not reach significance after site adjustment. No significant difference is a strong alternative.

answer: This is most likely a tissue-handling artifact, not CRPC biology. FOS, FOSB and EGR1 are immediate-early genes that rise within minutes of surgical manipulation, warm ischemia and ex vivo handling. Radical prostatectomy specimens are exposed to this stress response while the patient is still alive. Rapid-autopsy metastases come from deceased patients, where active transcription has stopped and the stress response is absent. So the 'decrease' in CRPC probably reflects induction in the prostatectomy samples. Checks: (1) Test whether other immediate-early and stress genes (JUN, JUNB, ATF3, IER2, IER3, DUSP1, NR4A1, KLF2/4/6, ZFP36, CYR61, EGR2/3) fall together in CRPC; a coordinated block points to handling. (2) Compare benign prostate tissue with localized cancer from the same prostatectomies; both should show high levels. (3) Within the CRPC group, compare metastatic sites (including any prostate-bed tissue taken at autopsy) to separate tissue-of-origin effects from collection method. (4) If annotations exist, look for correlation with ischemia time or post-mortem interval. (5) Check that the signal is not driven by the common reference or array batch. (6) Compare with datasets that use surgical metastases or biopsies (e.g., Taylor/MSKCC), or with published ischemia-time signatures.
ground_truth: 2 = identifies immediate-early gene induction from surgical warm ischemia / handling in prostatectomy samples (vs autopsy) and proposes checking co-variation with an IEG score or tissue-handling metadata; 1 = gives a plausible biological or composition argument without the handling artifact; 0 = treats it as a resistance driver.
expert_note: Correct: IEG induction from surgical ischemia in prostatectomy vs autopsy; proposes the IEG co-variation check used in section 4.
rationale: FOS, FOSB and EGR1 form a well-known ischemia- and handling-induced immediate-early signature that can confound prostatectomy versus autopsy comparisons.

answer: There is no SSTR1-selective drug in the clinic. The practical option is pasireotide (SOM230), the only approved "pan-somatostatin" analog, which binds SSTR1, 2, 3 and 5 (highest at SSTR5, then SSTR2/SSTR3, with sub-10 nM affinity at SSTR1) and essentially spares SSTR4. The classic analogs — octreotide, lanreotide, vapreotide — are SSTR2-preferring (SSTR2 >> SSTR5 ≈ SSTR3) and have negligible SSTR1 (and SSTR4) affinity; the same is true of the newer oral/non-peptide SSTR2 agonists (paltusotine) and of SSTR2-directed radioligands such as 68Ga/177Lu-DOTATATE and DOTATOC (DOTATOC/DOTANOC add some SSTR3/5 but not SSTR1). Native somatostatin-14/-28 and cortistatin bind all five receptors but are not therapeutically usable because of their seconds-long half-life. Truly SSTR1-preferring agonists (e.g., CH-275, L-797,591, des-AA1,2,5-[DTrp8,IAmp9]SST analogs) remain preclinical tool compounds. So for prostate-cancer experiments, pasireotide is the clinically available agent that engages SSTR1, but any SSTR1-attributed effect must be controlled against its SSTR2/3/5 activity — e.g., by comparing with octreotide/lanreotide, or by SSTR1 knockdown/subtype-selective tool agonists.
ground_truth: 2 = names pasireotide as the approved analog with meaningful SSTR1 affinity, states that octreotide and lanreotide bind SSTR1 weakly, and notes there is no approved SSTR1-selective agonist; 1 = partly correct; 0 = claims octreotide or lanreotide are SSTR1 agonists or invents a selective drug.
expert_note: Correct: pasireotide is the approved analog with SSTR1 affinity; octreotide/lanreotide negligible; no approved SSTR1-selective agonist. Answered by fallback model after a refusal.
rationale: Established pharmacology: pasireotide is the approved multi-receptor analog with SSTR1,2,3,5 affinity; octreotide/lanreotide and DOTATATE are SSTR2-preferring; SSTR1-selective agonists (CH-275, L-797,591) are preclinical only.

answer:
Do an isogenic gain-/loss-of-function enzalutamide sensitivity experiment.

Design: In matched pairs (LNCaP or C4-2B parental vs. their enzalutamide-resistant derivatives, e.g., C4-2B MDVR; confirm SSTR1 loss by qPCR/Western), (1) re-express SSTR1 in resistant cells using a doxycycline-inducible SSTR1 cDNA, and (2) knock down/knock out SSTR1 (two independent shRNAs/sgRNAs) in sensitive parental cells. Treat with an 8-point enzalutamide dose curve (plus DMSO vehicle) and measure viability at 5–7 days, plus 2-week colony formation; read out IC50/GI50 and AR target genes (KLK3, TMPRSS2, FKBP5).

Controls: empty vector/dox-only, non-targeting shRNA, sgSafe; rescue of knockdown with shRNA-resistant SSTR1; a signaling-dead SSTR1 mutant (DRY-motif) to show the effect requires receptor signaling; expression verification; equal dox exposure in all arms; ideally a second resistant model (22Rv1, LNCaP-AR) for generalizability.

Expected result if causal: SSTR1 re-expression lowers enzalutamide IC50 several-fold, reduces colony formation and restores AR-target suppression (resensitization), while SSTR1 knockdown in parental cells raises IC50 and sustains growth/AR signaling under enzalutamide; the signaling-dead mutant fails to resensitize. No IC50 shift in either direction would argue SSTR1 loss is a correlate, not a driver, prompting follow-up on it as a biomarker.
ground_truth: 2 = isogenic gain- and loss-of-function in an ARSI-sensitive and a matched resistant model, enzalutamide dose response as readout, rescue or ligand-dependence control, falsifiable prediction; 1 = reasonable but missing controls or causal logic; 0 = correlative only or infeasible.
expert_note: Sound isogenic GOF/LOF design with rescue and signaling-dead mutant. Misses a ligand arm: SSTR1 needs somatostatin or pasireotide, and culture media may lack ligand, so a null result could be a false negative. Answered by fallback model after a refusal.
rationale: The field-standard first causality test is bidirectional genetic manipulation in isogenic sensitive/resistant pairs with drug dose–response readouts, including rescue and signaling-dead controls. Confidence reflects that this is the canonical approach, though specific magnitude of effect is uncertain.
